subject: Science
title: Control and Coordination
summary: How animals and plants sense a change around them and respond to it: the nervous system (neuron, reflex arc, brain) and hormones in animals, and growth-based and non-growth movements plus plant hormones in plants. A scoring biology chapter with three diagrams the board keeps asking for.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark theory paper. This chapter sits in Unit II, World of Living (Chapters 5 to 8), which carries 25 marks. Control and Coordination alone typically fetches 4 to 6 marks: usually one or two 1-mark items plus one 3-mark or 5-mark question, and a diagram (neuron, reflex arc or human brain) is asked most years.

question_types.note: Location of receptors (gustatory, olfactory), which brain part does what, name of a plant hormone and its job, which gland secretes a hormone, the direction of signal flow at a synapse.
Reflex action versus voluntary action, cerebellum and balance, auxin on the shady side, iodine and thyroxine, insulin and diabetes.
Name the brain part for four given functions; difference between reflex action and walking; components of the peripheral nervous system; tropism definitions with one example.

Sequence of events in a reflex (bright light, hot object, sneezing); effect of adrenaline in a frightening situation; feedback control of insulin; why chemical communication is needed besides nerves; names and functions of plant hormones.

Draw and label a neuron, reflex arc or human brain and explain its working; diabetes case with hormone, gland and feedback; hydrotropism experiment plus plant hormones; nervous versus hormonal control.
A passage on blood-sugar regulation, a plant bending to light or Mimosa folding, followed by four short sub-questions.

hot_topics: Reflex arc: definition, sequence and labelled diagram
Structure of a neuron and how an impulse crosses a synapse
Parts of the human brain and their functions (cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla, pons)
Phototropism and the role of auxin; other tropisms with examples
Plant hormones: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid
Adrenaline response and insulin feedback mechanism
Endocrine glands, their hormones and deficiency effects (dwarfism, goitre, diabetes)
Nervous control versus hormonal control; Mimosa movement versus muscle movement

sections.heading: Introduction: why control and coordination is needed
sections.body:
Chapter 5 told you that movement is a sign of life. This chapter asks a sharper question: how does an organism decide to move? A living thing moves in response to a change in its surroundings. Such a change that the organism can detect is called a stimulus: heat, light, touch, a chemical, gravity. The movement that follows is the response. Because a response must be exactly matched to the stimulus (you pull your hand from a hot pan, you do not pull it from a cold one), the body needs a system that detects the change, decides on the response and then makes the right part of the body act. That system is what we call control and coordination.

In animals, two kinds of tissue do this job together. Nervous tissue carries information quickly as electrical impulses, and muscular tissue produces the actual movement. Alongside the nerves, animals also use chemical messengers called hormones, which travel in the blood and give slower but longer-lasting control. Plants have no nervous system or muscles at all, yet a sensitive plant folds its leaves the moment you touch it and every seedling sends its root down and its shoot up. Plants manage this by chemical signals and by changing the shape or growth rate of their cells.

The examiner likes NCERT exercise question 9, which asks why an organism needs such a system at all. The two-line answer is: to receive stimuli from the environment and from inside the body, and to produce a suitable, coordinated response so that all organs work together for the survival of the organism.
sections.tip: Keep the words stimulus, receptor, response and effector ready. Almost every 2-mark question in this chapter can be answered by placing them in the right order.

sections.heading: 6.1 Animals – Nervous System (receptors, neuron and synapse)
sections.body:
Information about the environment first has to be picked up. This is done by receptors, which are specialised tips of nerve cells sitting in our sense organs. Two receptors are named in NCERT and are asked almost every year: gustatory receptors on the tongue detect taste, and olfactory receptors in the nose detect smell. The skin has receptors for touch, heat and pain; the eye for light; the ear for sound.

The unit of the nervous system is the neuron (nerve cell). It has three parts you must be able to draw and name. The dendrites are short, branched fibres that receive information. The cell body (cyton) contains the nucleus and cytoplasm. The axon is the single longest fibre; it carries the impulse away from the cell body and ends in fine branches called nerve endings.

Now the working. Information picked up at the dendritic tip sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. This impulse travels along the dendrite to the cell body, then along the axon to its end. At the end of the axon the electrical impulse causes the release of certain chemicals. These chemicals cross the tiny gap between the axon end of one neuron and the dendrite of the next, called the synapse, and start a fresh electrical impulse in the next neuron. In the same way, the impulse is finally passed from a neuron to a muscle cell or a gland, which then acts.

A favourite 3-mark question (CBSE 2019) asks why the signal crosses a synapse only from the axonal end of one neuron to the dendritic end of the next and not in reverse. The answer: the chemicals are released only at the axon end, and the receptors for those chemicals are present only on the dendrite of the next neuron. So the impulse can travel in one direction only.
sections.tip: In the neuron diagram, draw the arrow of impulse from dendrite to axon end. An arrow in the wrong direction costs a mark even if all labels are right.

sections.heading: 6.1.1 What happens in Reflex Actions?
sections.body:
A reflex action is a sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, made without conscious thought. Touching a flame, sneezing, blinking when something comes near the eye, the knee jerk: all are reflexes. The whole point of a reflex is speed. If the signal had to go up to the brain, be thought about and then come back, your hand would be burnt by the time you moved it.

The pathway a reflex follows is the reflex arc. Learn the sequence exactly as the marking scheme wants it: Receptor (heat receptor in the skin) → sensory neuron (afferent) carries the impulse to the spinal cord → a relay neuron (interneuron) inside the spinal cord passes it to a motor neuron (efferent) → the motor neuron carries the impulse to the effector (muscle of the arm), which contracts and pulls the hand away. Nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle in the spinal cord on their way to the brain, so the spinal cord is the natural place for such short-cut connections. The reflex arc is therefore formed in the spinal cord, although information about the event also goes on to the brain, which is why you become aware of the pain a moment later.

Two comparisons recur in papers. Reflex action versus walking (NCERT in-text): a reflex is involuntary, very fast and controlled by the spinal cord; walking is voluntary, slower and controlled by the brain (cerebrum decides, cerebellum coordinates). Reflex action versus involuntary action (NCERT exercise 10): both happen without conscious control, but a reflex is a response to an external stimulus and is handled mainly by the spinal cord, whereas an involuntary action such as heartbeat or digestion runs continuously without an external stimulus and is controlled by the mid-brain and hind-brain (medulla).

NCERT also points out that reflex arcs evolved in animals because the thinking part of the brain is not fast enough for emergencies, and that even in animals with a complex brain the arcs stay because they remain more efficient for quick responses.
sections.tip: For the sneezing or bright-light sequence question, write it as a flowchart with arrows: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector → response. Name the actual receptor and effector for that case.

sections.heading: 6.1.2 Human Brain
sections.body:
The spinal cord handles reflexes, but thinking, remembering and most voluntary actions need the brain. Together, the brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system (CNS). The CNS talks to the rest of the body through the peripheral nervous system (PNS), which is made of cranial nerves arising from the brain and spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord. The 2016 two-marker asked exactly this: name the two components of the PNS.

The brain has three main regions. The fore-brain is the largest part and its main structure is the cerebrum, the thinking part. It has separate sensory areas that receive information from the receptors for hearing, smell, sight and so on; association areas that put this information together with what is already stored and decide what to do; and motor areas that send the decision to the muscles. The sensation of feeling full after a meal comes from a centre associated with hunger, also in the fore-brain.

The mid-brain and the hind-brain together control many involuntary actions. The hind-brain has three parts you must know. The medulla controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation, vomiting and heartbeat. The cerebellum is responsible for the precision of voluntary actions and for maintaining posture and balance; walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle or picking up a pencil all depend on it. The pons lies between the medulla and the mid-brain and helps regulate breathing.

A 2023 two-marker listed four activities and asked for the brain part: posture and balance (cerebellum), heartbeat (medulla), thinking (cerebrum), blood pressure (medulla). A 2018 three-marker did the same with feeling full (fore-brain), vomiting (medulla), picking up a pencil and riding a bicycle (cerebellum). Practise these mappings until they are automatic; they are the cheapest marks in the chapter.
sections.tip: The brain diagram in NCERT (Fig. 6.3) shows cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla, pons and spinal cord, with the pituitary gland hanging below the fore-brain. Draw it side-on and label at least those six.

sections.heading: 6.1.3 How are these Tissues protected?
sections.body:
Nervous tissue is delicate, and the brain and spinal cord are so important that the body gives them the best protection it has. The brain sits inside a bony box, the skull (cranium). Inside the skull, the brain is contained in a fluid-filled balloon: the cerebrospinal fluid surrounds the brain and acts as a shock absorber, so that a knock on the head does not transmit the jolt straight to the soft tissue. The spinal cord runs down inside the vertebral column, or backbone, a chain of bones that guards it the way the skull guards the brain.

This section is small but it produces reliable 1-mark and 2-mark questions: how is the brain protected, how is the spinal cord protected, what is the function of the cranium and the vertebral column. Write both the bony covering and the fluid when asked about the brain; many students mention only the skull and lose a mark.

The section also connects to NCERT exercise question 7 on spinal-cord injury. Since sensory impulses travel up the spinal cord to the brain and motor impulses travel down from the brain to the muscles, an injury to the spinal cord disrupts both: reflex actions whose arcs are formed at or below the injured level are lost, and voluntary signals from the brain cannot reach the muscles below the injury, so the person may lose sensation and movement in those parts.
sections.tip: Cranium protects the brain; vertebral column protects the spinal cord; cerebrospinal fluid absorbs shock. Three phrases, three marks.

sections.heading: 6.1.4 How does the Nervous Tissue cause Action?
sections.body:
Detecting a stimulus and deciding on a response is useless unless something actually moves. The final step of nervous control is a muscle. When a nerve impulse reaches a muscle, the muscle fibre must move, and the only way a cell can move is by changing its shape. NCERT explains it simply: muscle cells contain special proteins that change both their shape and their arrangement inside the cell in response to the electrical impulse arriving from the nerve. The new arrangement of these proteins makes the muscle cell shorter. A whole muscle made of such cells therefore contracts, pulls on the bone it is attached to, and the limb moves.

This is the answer to the second half of the 2020 five-marker about a cheetah chasing prey: seeing the prey, the cheetah's nervous system sends impulses to the leg muscles; the muscle proteins change shape and arrangement, the cells shorten, and the legs move. At the same time adrenaline (Section 6.3) raises the heart rate and diverts blood to the muscles so that they receive more oxygen and glucose.

The same idea distinguishes animal movement from plant movement, a comparison asked in NCERT exercise 12 and in papers. In our legs, movement is due to muscle contraction driven by nerve impulses and controlled by the brain; the cell does not change its water content. In the sensitive plant, there are no nerves or muscles; the leaf cells change shape by gaining or losing water. Keep this section in mind when you reach 6.2.1.
sections.tip: If asked how a muscle moves, the key phrase is: special proteins change their shape and arrangement, so the muscle cell becomes shorter. Do not write about actin and myosin filaments unless you are sure; NCERT does not name them.

sections.heading: 6.2 Coordination in Plants and 6.2.1 Immediate Response to Stimulus
sections.body:
Plants have no nervous system and no muscles, yet they respond to their surroundings. NCERT opens with two examples. Touch the leaves of the sensitive plant, Mimosa pudica (chhui-mui), and they fold up and droop within seconds. Plant a seed, and however you lay it, the root grows down and the shoot grows up. These are two different kinds of movement. The Mimosa movement is independent of growth; the seedling movement is due to growth. The chapter treats them separately.

Take the immediate response first. The Mimosa leaf moves at the point of touch, so something must carry the information from the touched cells to the cells that move. Plants use electrical-chemical means to pass information from cell to cell, but they have no specialised tissue for conducting it, unlike our nerves. And to move, the plant cannot use muscle proteins. Instead the cells at the base of the leaflets change the amount of water in them. Losing water makes the cells shrink, gaining water makes them swell, and this change in shape folds or opens the leaf. The response is quick, does not depend on the direction of the stimulus, and does not involve growth.

This gives the standard comparison asked as an NCERT in-text question and in CBSE 2023: movement of Mimosa leaves versus movement of a shoot towards light. Mimosa: caused by touch, not directional, not a growth movement, occurs by change in water content of cells, rapid. Shoot towards light: caused by light, directional (towards the stimulus), a growth movement, occurs by unequal growth due to auxin, slow.

Movements like the Mimosa response that do not depend on the direction of the stimulus are called nastic movements; the Mimosa touch response is a thigmonastic movement. Directional growth movements are tropisms, which come next.
sections.tip: Two words separate the two plant movements: water (Mimosa, fast, non-directional) and growth (tropism, slow, directional). Anchor every comparison on these two.

sections.heading: 6.2.2 Movement Due to Growth (tropisms and plant hormones)
sections.body:
Some plant movements are really just differential growth: one side of an organ grows faster than the other, so the organ bends. A tendril of a pea plant is the simplest case. When the tendril touches a support, the side in contact grows more slowly than the side away from it, so the tendril curls around the support. Directional growth movements in response to a stimulus are called tropic movements or tropisms. Growth towards the stimulus is positive, away from it negative.

Learn the four tropisms with the examples the examiner expects. Phototropism, response to light: shoots are positively phototropic, roots negatively. Geotropism (gravitropism), response to gravity: roots grow downward (positive), shoots upward (negative). Hydrotropism, response to water: roots grow towards water. Chemotropism, response to a chemical: growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule is the standard example.

How does a plant know which side to grow on? Through plant hormones (phytohormones), chemical compounds made in one part of the plant that diffuse to another and regulate growth. The board's favourite explanation is phototropism. Auxin is synthesised at the shoot tip and helps cells grow longer. When light falls on one side of the shoot, auxin diffuses towards the shady side. The higher concentration of auxin there makes the cells on the shady side elongate more than those on the lit side, so the shoot bends towards the light. Write these four steps and you have the 3-mark answer.

Four hormones are named in NCERT. Auxin: cell elongation, phototropism, coiling of tendrils. Gibberellins: help in growth of the stem. Cytokinins: promote cell division, so they are found in high concentration in fruits and seeds where cells divide rapidly. Abscisic acid: the growth inhibitor; its effects include wilting of leaves. A 2019 Delhi question asked you to name the hormone for growth (gibberellin), cell division (cytokinin), inhibition (abscisic acid) and elongation (auxin), so keep each one attached to its single job.

NCERT also asks you to design an experiment for hydrotropism. Take two trays of moist soil with seedlings. In one, bury a porous clay pot filled with water near one side. After a few days the roots in that tray are seen growing towards the pot, while the roots in the control tray grow straight down.
sections.tip: For any tropism diagram, draw the stimulus (light source, water pot, ground level) and the organ bending, and label the side with more auxin. A diagram without the stimulus marked earns half credit.

sections.heading: 6.3 Hormones in Animals
sections.body:
Nerves are fast but they have limits: an impulse reaches only the cells connected to nervous tissue, and a cell cannot fire impulses continuously; it must reset before the next one. So animals also use chemical communication. A cell releases a chemical, called a hormone, into the blood; it is carried to the whole body and acts on target cells that can detect it. Hormones are made by endocrine glands (ductless glands, which pour their secretion directly into the blood). This is the answer to the 2020 question on why chemical communication is better than electrical impulses.

Adrenaline from the adrenal glands is the model example. When you are frightened or excited, adrenaline is secreted into the blood and prepares the body to fight or run: the heart beats faster so more oxygen reaches the muscles; the small arteries of the digestive system and skin contract, diverting blood to the skeletal muscles; and the breathing rate rises because the diaphragm and rib muscles contract faster. The squirrel-in-danger (CBSE 2020) and scary-situation (CBSE 2023) questions want exactly these three changes.

Other hormones you must know with gland, function and deficiency effect. Growth hormone from the pituitary regulates growth and development; deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism. Thyroxine from the thyroid regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism for balanced growth; the gland needs iodine to make it, so iodine deficiency causes goitre, seen as a swollen neck, which is why iodised salt is advised. Testosterone from the testes in males and oestrogen from the ovaries in females bring about the changes of puberty. Insulin from the pancreas regulates blood sugar; too little insulin lets blood sugar rise, causing diabetes, which is why some patients are treated with insulin injections.

Finally, timing and amount are controlled by feedback. When blood sugar rises, the cells of the pancreas detect it and secrete more insulin; as sugar falls, insulin secretion is reduced. This 3-mark feedback question (CBSE 2019) is asked in many disguises.
sections.tip: For every hormone, write a three-part line: gland, function, what goes wrong without it. The marking scheme gives separate marks for each part.

key_terms.definition: Any change in the surroundings or inside the body that an organism can detect and respond to, such as light, heat, touch, gravity or a chemical.
A specialised tip of a nerve cell, usually in a sense organ, that detects a particular stimulus. Gustatory receptors (tongue) detect taste; olfactory receptors (nose) detect smell.
The structural and functional unit of the nervous system, made of dendrites (receive impulse), cell body with nucleus, and a single long axon ending in nerve endings.
The tiny gap between the axon end of one neuron and the dendrite of the next, across which the impulse is carried by chemicals released at the axon end.
A sudden, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that is controlled by the spinal cord without conscious thought, such as withdrawing the hand from a flame.
The path followed by an impulse in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector.
The muscle or gland that carries out the response when a motor neuron delivers an impulse to it.
The brain and the spinal cord together; the site where information is processed and responses are decided.
The cranial nerves arising from the brain and the spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord, which connect the central nervous system to the rest of the body.
Part of the hind-brain responsible for the precision of voluntary actions and for maintaining the posture and balance of the body.
Part of the hind-brain that controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, heartbeat, salivation and vomiting.
A directional growth movement of a plant part towards or away from a stimulus such as light, gravity, water or a chemical.
A plant movement that is independent of the direction of the stimulus and does not involve growth, such as the folding of Mimosa leaves on touch.
Growth of a plant part in response to light; shoots bend towards light (positive), roots grow away from it (negative).
Growth of a plant part in response to gravity; roots grow downward (positive), shoots grow upward (negative).
A plant hormone synthesised at the shoot tip that makes cells grow longer; it diffuses to the shady side of a shoot and causes bending towards light.
A chemical messenger secreted in small amounts by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which acts on target cells elsewhere in the body.
A ductless gland that releases its hormone directly into the blood, for example the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands and pancreas.
The way the amount and timing of a hormone are regulated by its own effect; a rise in blood sugar makes the pancreas secrete more insulin, and the fall in sugar reduces secretion.
Swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck caused by deficiency of iodine, which is needed to synthesise thyroxine.

formula_sheet.name: Impulse path inside a neuron
formula_sheet.expr: Dendrite → cell body → axon → axon end (nerve ending) → chemicals released → next dendrite
formula_sheet.note: One direction only; the impulse is electrical inside the neuron and chemical at the synapse.

formula_sheet.name: Reflex arc sequence
formula_sheet.expr: Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle or gland)
formula_sheet.note: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord; information still goes to the brain afterwards.

formula_sheet.name: Divisions of the nervous system
formula_sheet.expr: CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = cranial nerves (from brain) + spinal nerves (from spinal cord)
formula_sheet.note: Asked as a 1- or 2-mark direct question.

formula_sheet.name: Brain parts and jobs
formula_sheet.expr: Cerebrum: thinking, memory, voluntary action; Cerebellum: precision, posture, balance; Medulla: blood pressure, heartbeat, salivation, vomiting; Pons: regulates breathing
formula_sheet.note: Cerebrum is in the fore-brain; cerebellum, medulla and pons are in the hind-brain.

formula_sheet.name: Protection of nervous tissue
formula_sheet.expr: Brain: skull (cranium) + cerebrospinal fluid as shock absorber; Spinal cord: vertebral column
formula_sheet.note: Mention the fluid as well as the bone for full marks.

formula_sheet.name: Tropisms and examples
formula_sheet.expr: Phototropism: shoot + / root −; Geotropism: root + / shoot −; Hydrotropism: root +; Chemotropism: pollen tube towards ovule
formula_sheet.note: Plus sign means growth towards the stimulus.

formula_sheet.name: Plant hormones
formula_sheet.expr: Auxin: cell elongation, phototropism, tendril coiling; Gibberellin: stem growth; Cytokinin: cell division (fruits, seeds); Abscisic acid: inhibits growth, wilting of leaves
formula_sheet.note: Auxin is made at the shoot tip and diffuses to the shady side.

formula_sheet.name: Adrenaline response
formula_sheet.expr: Heart rate ↑ → more O<sub>2</sub> to muscles; arteries to gut and skin contract → blood diverted to skeletal muscles; breathing rate ↑
formula_sheet.note: Secreted by adrenal glands directly into blood in fear or excitement.

formula_sheet.name: Hormone, gland and deficiency
formula_sheet.expr: Growth hormone (pituitary) → dwarfism; Thyroxine (thyroid, needs iodine) → goitre; Insulin (pancreas) → diabetes; Testosterone (testes), Oestrogen (ovaries) → puberty changes
formula_sheet.note: Write gland, function and deficiency disease as three separate points.

formula_sheet.name: Insulin feedback
formula_sheet.expr: Blood sugar ↑ → pancreas secretes more insulin → sugar ↓ → insulin secretion reduced
formula_sheet.note: The standard example of feedback control of hormone secretion.

diagrams.title: Structure of a neuron (NCERT Fig. 6.1a)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a star-shaped cell body with a nucleus inside and several short branched dendrites coming off it. From one side draw a single long axon, much longer than the dendrites, ending in a tuft of fine nerve endings. Label dendrite, cell body, nucleus, axon and nerve ending, and draw an arrow along the axon showing the direction of impulse from dendrites towards the nerve ending.

diagrams.title: Reflex arc (NCERT Fig. 6.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a cross-section of the spinal cord (butterfly-shaped grey matter inside an oval) with a hand near a flame on one side. Show a sensory neuron running from the heat receptor in the skin into the spinal cord, a relay neuron inside the spinal cord, and a motor neuron leaving the spinal cord to the muscle of the arm. Label receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and effector (muscle), and mark arrows in the direction receptor to effector. Add a short arrow from the spinal cord upward labelled to brain.

diagrams.title: Human brain (NCERT Fig. 6.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a side view: a large, wrinkled cerebrum at the top and front, a smaller wrinkled cerebellum at the back below it, the pons as a bulge in front of the cerebellum, the medulla below the pons narrowing into the spinal cord, and the pituitary gland hanging from the underside of the fore-brain on a short stalk. Label cerebrum, cerebellum, pons, medulla, pituitary gland and spinal cord, and bracket the regions as fore-brain, mid-brain and hind-brain.

diagrams.title: Phototropism in a shoot (NCERT Fig. 6.6)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a shoot in a pot with light arrows coming from one side, and the shoot bending towards the light. Show dots representing auxin concentrated on the shady side of the shoot tip and write that cells on the shady side elongate more. Label light source, shoot tip (site of auxin synthesis), shady side with more auxin, and direction of bending.

diagrams.title: Geotropism in a plant
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a potted plant laid on its side (or a seedling placed horizontally). Show the shoot curving upward, away from gravity, and the root curving downward, towards gravity. Label the shoot as negatively geotropic, the root as positively geotropic, and draw an arrow marked gravity pointing down.

diagrams.title: Endocrine glands in the human body (NCERT Fig. 6.10)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a simple outline of the human body and mark, from top to bottom: pituitary gland (base of brain), thyroid gland (in the neck), adrenal glands (on top of the two kidneys), pancreas (below the stomach), and testes (male) or ovaries (female). Write the main hormone beside each: growth hormone, thyroxine, adrenaline, insulin, testosterone or oestrogen.

ncert_questions.q: What is the difference between a reflex action and walking?
ncert_questions.a: A reflex action is a sudden, involuntary and automatic response to a stimulus (for example, withdrawing the hand from a hot object). It is controlled by the spinal cord through a reflex arc, needs no thinking and is very fast. Walking is a voluntary action: it is decided and controlled by the brain (cerebrum for the decision, cerebellum for coordination and balance), can be started or stopped at will and is slower because the impulse travels to the brain and back.

ncert_questions.q: What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
ncert_questions.a: A synapse is the gap between the axon end of one neuron and the dendrite of the next. When the electrical impulse reaches the axon end, it causes the release of chemicals into the gap. These chemicals diffuse across the synapse and start a fresh electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. In this way the impulse is passed from one neuron to the next, and finally from a neuron to a muscle or gland. Transmission is one-way because the chemicals are released only at the axon end.

ncert_questions.q: Which part of the brain maintains posture and equilibrium of the body?
ncert_questions.a: The cerebellum, a part of the hind-brain, maintains posture and balance (equilibrium) of the body and is responsible for the precision of voluntary actions such as walking in a straight line or riding a bicycle.

ncert_questions.q: How do we detect the smell of an agarbatti (incense stick)?
ncert_questions.a: Smell is detected by olfactory receptors present in the nose. The chemicals from the burning agarbatti reach these receptors and set off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. The impulse travels along the sensory neurons to the olfactory (smell) area in the fore-brain (cerebrum), where the sensation is interpreted as the smell of the agarbatti.

ncert_questions.q: What is the role of the brain in reflex action?
ncert_questions.a: A reflex action is generated by the spinal cord through the reflex arc, so the brain does not decide the response. However, the information about the stimulus is also sent to the brain after the reflex, so the brain becomes aware of what happened (we feel the pain after pulling the hand away) and can store the experience and take further voluntary action.

ncert_questions.q: What are plant hormones?
ncert_questions.a: Plant hormones, or phytohormones, are chemical compounds produced in one part of a plant and diffused to other parts, where they coordinate growth, development and responses to the environment. Examples are auxin (cell elongation), gibberellin (stem growth), cytokinin (cell division) and abscisic acid (inhibits growth, causes wilting of leaves).

ncert_questions.q: How is the movement of leaves of the sensitive plant different from the movement of a shoot towards light?
ncert_questions.a: Movement of Mimosa leaves: it is a response to touch; it is not directional (does not depend on the direction of the stimulus); it is not a growth movement; it occurs because the cells at the base of the leaflets change their water content and so change shape; it is rapid. Movement of a shoot towards light: it is a response to light; it is directional (towards the stimulus); it is a growth movement (tropism); it occurs because auxin makes cells on the shady side elongate more; it is slow.

ncert_questions.q: Give an example of a plant hormone that promotes growth.
ncert_questions.a: Auxin promotes growth by causing cells to elongate; gibberellins promote the growth of the stem; cytokinins promote cell division. Any one of these is accepted, auxin being the usual answer.

ncert_questions.q: How do auxins promote the growth of a tendril around a support?
ncert_questions.a: When a tendril comes in contact with a support, auxin moves away from the side touching the support to the side away from it. Auxin makes cells grow longer, so the side of the tendril away from the support grows faster than the side in contact with it. This unequal growth makes the tendril bend and coil around the support.

ncert_questions.q: Design an experiment to demonstrate hydrotropism.
ncert_questions.a: Take two trays filled with moist soil and plant a few seedlings in each. In tray A bury a porous clay pot filled with water near one side; leave tray B without a pot as the control. Keep both trays in identical conditions for a few days. Observation: in tray A the roots bend and grow towards the porous pot, that is, towards the water; in tray B the roots grow straight down. Conclusion: roots grow towards water, showing positive hydrotropism.

ncert_questions.q: How does chemical coordination take place in animals?
ncert_questions.a: Chemical coordination in animals takes place through hormones. Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the blood, which carries them to every part of the body. Target cells that can detect a particular hormone respond to it. For example, when an animal is frightened, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which raises the heart rate and breathing rate and diverts blood to the muscles. The amount and timing of secretion are regulated by feedback, as when a rise in blood sugar makes the pancreas release more insulin.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the use of iodised salt advisable?
ncert_questions.a: Iodine is essential for the thyroid gland to synthesise the hormone thyroxine, which regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism for balanced growth. If the diet lacks iodine, thyroxine cannot be made properly and the thyroid may swell, causing goitre (a swollen neck). Iodised salt supplies this iodine in the daily diet and prevents goitre.

ncert_questions.q: How does our body respond when adrenaline is secreted into the blood?
ncert_questions.a: Adrenaline prepares the body to deal with an emergency. The heart beats faster, so more oxygen is supplied to the muscles. The small arteries of the digestive system and the skin contract, so blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles. The breathing rate increases because the diaphragm and rib muscles contract faster. Together these changes let the body fight or run.

ncert_questions.q: Why are some patients with diabetes treated by giving injections of insulin?
ncert_questions.a: Insulin, secreted by the pancreas, regulates the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood. In diabetes the pancreas does not secrete enough insulin, so blood sugar rises and causes harmful effects. Injecting insulin supplies the missing hormone and brings the blood sugar back under control. It is given as an injection, not as a tablet, because insulin is a protein and would be digested in the stomach.

ncert_questions.q: Which of the following is a plant hormone? (a) Insulin (b) Thyroxin (c) Oestrogen (d) Cytokinin
ncert_questions.a: (d) Cytokinin. Insulin, thyroxin and oestrogen are all animal hormones secreted by the pancreas, thyroid and ovaries respectively. Cytokinin is a plant hormone that promotes cell division.

ncert_questions.q: The gap between two neurons is called a (a) dendrite (b) synapse (c) axon (d) impulse
ncert_questions.a: (b) Synapse. The dendrite and axon are parts of a neuron and the impulse is the signal that travels along it; the gap across which the impulse passes chemically from one neuron to the next is the synapse.

ncert_questions.q: The brain is responsible for (a) thinking (b) regulating the heart beat (c) balancing the body (d) all of the above
ncert_questions.a: (d) All of the above. Thinking is done by the cerebrum (fore-brain), heartbeat is regulated by the medulla (hind-brain) and balance is maintained by the cerebellum (hind-brain).

ncert_questions.q: What is the function of receptors in our body? Think of situations where receptors do not work properly. What problems are likely to arise?
ncert_questions.a: Receptors are specialised tips of nerve cells located in sense organs that detect a stimulus from the environment (light, sound, smell, taste, heat, touch) and convert it into an electrical impulse, which is sent to the central nervous system so that a response can be made. If receptors do not work properly the body cannot sense the stimulus and cannot respond. For example, if the heat receptors of the skin fail, a person would not withdraw the hand from a hot object and would be burnt; if olfactory receptors fail, a person cannot smell leaking gas or spoilt food; if gustatory receptors fail, taste is lost.

ncert_questions.q: Draw the structure of a neuron and explain its function.
ncert_questions.a: Draw the neuron with dendrites, cell body containing the nucleus, a long axon and nerve endings, with an arrow showing the direction of the impulse. Function: the dendrites receive information from a receptor or another neuron and set off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. The impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body and along the axon to its end. At the axon end, chemicals are released that cross the synapse and start a similar impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron, or in a muscle or gland. Thus the neuron receives, conducts and transmits nerve impulses.

ncert_questions.q: How does phototropism occur in plants?
ncert_questions.a: Phototropism is the bending of a plant part in response to light; shoots bend towards light. Auxin is synthesised at the shoot tip and helps the cells grow longer. When light falls on one side of the shoot, auxin diffuses towards the shady side. The higher concentration of auxin on the shady side stimulates those cells to elongate more than the cells on the lit side. Because of this unequal growth the shoot bends towards the light.

ncert_questions.q: Which signals will get disrupted in case of a spinal cord injury?
ncert_questions.a: The spinal cord carries sensory impulses from receptors up to the brain and motor impulses from the brain down to the effectors, and reflex arcs are formed in it. An injury to the spinal cord therefore disrupts (i) reflex actions whose arcs pass through the injured region, (ii) sensory signals from parts of the body below the injury to the brain, so sensation is lost, and (iii) motor signals from the brain to muscles below the injury, so voluntary movement is lost.

ncert_questions.q: How does chemical coordination occur in plants?
ncert_questions.a: Plants coordinate growth and responses using plant hormones (phytohormones), chemicals made in one part of the plant and diffused to the part where they act. Auxin, made at the shoot tip, causes cell elongation and is responsible for phototropism and coiling of tendrils. Gibberellins help in the growth of the stem. Cytokinins promote cell division and are abundant in fruits and seeds. Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves. By varying where and how much of these hormones is present, the plant grows towards or away from a stimulus.

ncert_questions.q: What is the need for a system of control and coordination in an organism?
ncert_questions.a: An organism lives in a changing environment and must respond to changes (stimuli) in a way that helps it survive: moving away from danger, towards food or light, and keeping its internal conditions steady. A multicellular body has many organs, and their activities must be linked so that they work together. The nervous system and hormones provide this control and coordination: they detect stimuli, decide the response and make the right organs act at the right time in the right amount.

ncert_questions.q: How are involuntary actions and reflex actions different from each other?
ncert_questions.a: Both occur without conscious control, but: a reflex action is a rapid response to a specific external stimulus (withdrawing the hand from a flame, sneezing) and is controlled by the spinal cord through a reflex arc; an involuntary action runs continuously without a specific external stimulus (heartbeat, breathing, digestion, salivation) and is controlled by the mid-brain and hind-brain (medulla). Reflexes are occasional; involuntary actions go on all the time.

ncert_questions.q: Compare and contrast nervous and hormonal mechanisms for control and coordination in animals.
ncert_questions.a: Both are systems that coordinate the body's response to stimuli and both work together (for example, the brain and the pituitary). Differences: nervous control uses electrical impulses along neurons; hormonal control uses chemicals carried in the blood. Nervous response is very fast; hormonal response is slower. Nervous effect is short-lived; hormonal effect lasts longer. Nervous signals reach only cells connected to nervous tissue; hormones reach every cell but act only on target cells. A neuron must reset before firing again; hormones can be secreted continuously. Nervous control does not affect growth; hormones control growth and development.

ncert_questions.q: What is the difference between the manner in which movement takes place in a sensitive plant and the movement in our legs?
ncert_questions.a: In the sensitive plant, movement is a response to touch and happens because the cells at the base of the leaves change the amount of water in them, so they swell or shrink and change shape; there are no nerves or muscles, the information is passed by electrical-chemical means without any specialised tissue, and the movement is involuntary. In our legs, movement is caused by muscle contraction: nerve impulses from the brain reach the muscle, special proteins in the muscle cells change their shape and arrangement, the cells shorten and the leg moves; it is a voluntary action controlled by the nervous system and does not involve a change in the water content of cells.

pyq.q: The cerebellum is a part of the hind-brain. Which of the following actions is controlled by the cerebellum?
options: Change in the size of the pupil
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The cerebellum is responsible for the precision of voluntary actions and for posture and balance, so riding a bicycle depends on it. Pupil size, salivation and vomiting are involuntary actions controlled by the mid-brain and medulla.

pyq.q: Gustatory receptors are present in the:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Gustatory receptors detect taste and are located on the tongue. Olfactory receptors, which detect smell, are in the nose.

pyq.q: Rajesh noticed that a potted plant kept near the window of his room bends towards the sunlight. This is because:
options: Auxin accumulates on the lit side and makes those cells grow longer
Auxin diffuses to the shady side and makes those cells grow longer
Cytokinin causes rapid cell division on the lit side
Abscisic acid inhibits growth on the shady side
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Auxin made at the shoot tip diffuses to the shady side; the cells there elongate more than those on the lit side, so the shoot bends towards light.

pyq.q: In plants, the role of cytokinin is to:
options: Help in growth of the stem
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Cytokinins promote cell division, which is why they are found in higher concentration in fruits and seeds. Growth inhibition and wilting are effects of abscisic acid; stem growth is due to gibberellins.

pyq.q: The sensory neuron of a reflex arc carries information from the receptor to the:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In a reflex arc the sensory neuron carries the impulse from the receptor to the spinal cord, where a relay neuron passes it to the motor neuron.

pyq.q: At a synapse, the chemical signal is transmitted from the:
options: Axonal end of one neuron to the dendritic end of the next neuron
Dendritic end of one neuron to the axonal end of the next neuron
Cell body of one neuron to the cell body of the next neuron
Dendritic end of one neuron to the dendritic end of the next neuron
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Chemicals are released only at the axon end and are received only by the dendrite of the next neuron, so transmission is one-way from axon to dendrite.

pyq.q: Deficiency of which hormone in childhood leads to dwarfism?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Growth hormone, secreted by the pituitary gland, regulates growth and development; its deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism.

pyq.q: Which part of the brain controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The medulla in the hind-brain controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Reflex actions are faster than voluntary actions. Reason (R): Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord, so the impulse does not have to travel to the brain before the response is produced.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Reflexes are fast precisely because the arc is completed in the spinal cord and the thinking part of the brain is bypassed, so R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Abscisic acid promotes the growth of the stem in plants. Reason (R): Gibberellins help in the growth of the stem.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves, so A is false. Gibberellins do help in stem growth, so R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The roots of a plant are positively geotropic. Reason (R): The roots of a plant grow away from light.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true: roots grow towards gravity and away from light. But growing downward is a response to gravity, not to light, so R does not explain A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Use of iodised salt is advised in the diet. Reason (R): Iodine is essential for the thyroid gland to synthesise thyroxine.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Iodised salt supplies iodine, without which thyroxine cannot be made and goitre develops; R is the reason for A.

pyq.q: Rahul saw a snake and immediately jumped away from it. A little later, he walked away calmly from the spot. How do the two actions differ?
pyq.answer: Jumping away on seeing the snake is a reflex action: it is involuntary, automatic and very fast, produced by a reflex arc in the spinal cord without conscious thought. Walking away later is a voluntary action: it is decided by the brain (cerebrum) after thinking, is slower and is under his conscious control. (1 mark each.)

pyq.q: Name the part of the human brain responsible for (i) maintaining posture and balance, (ii) regulating heartbeat, (iii) thinking, (iv) controlling blood pressure.
pyq.answer: (i) Cerebellum. (ii) Medulla (hind-brain). (iii) Cerebrum (fore-brain). (iv) Medulla (hind-brain). Half a mark each.

pyq.q: (a) Name the two components of the peripheral nervous system. (b) Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure and salivation?
pyq.answer: (a) Cranial nerves, which arise from the brain, and spinal nerves, which arise from the spinal cord. (1 mark) (b) The medulla, in the hind-brain. (1 mark)

pyq.q: (a) Name the mineral required by the thyroid gland to synthesise its hormone. (b) State one way of preventing the deficiency disease that results when this mineral is lacking.
pyq.answer: (a) Iodine is required by the thyroid gland to synthesise thyroxine. (1 mark) (b) Deficiency of iodine causes goitre (swollen neck). It is prevented by using iodised salt in the diet, which supplies iodine. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Define tropic movements. Give one example each of positive and negative phototropism.
pyq.answer: Tropic movements (tropisms) are directional growth movements of a plant part towards or away from a stimulus such as light, gravity, water or a chemical. (1 mark) Positive phototropism: the shoot bends and grows towards light. Negative phototropism: the root grows away from light. (½ mark each)

pyq.q: A squirrel is in a scary situation. Its body has to prepare either to fight or to run away. State the immediate changes that take place in its body so that it is able to do so, and name the hormone responsible.
pyq.answer: The hormone is adrenaline, secreted by the adrenal glands directly into the blood. (1 mark) Immediate changes: (i) the heart beats faster, so more oxygen is supplied to the muscles; (ii) the small arteries of the digestive system and skin contract, so blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles; (iii) the breathing rate increases because the diaphragm and rib muscles contract faster. (2 marks) These changes give the muscles the oxygen and energy needed to fight or flee.

pyq.q: Define reflex arc. Trace the sequence of events that occur when a bright light is focused on your eyes.
pyq.answer: A reflex arc is the path along which the nerve impulse travels in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron (in the spinal cord or brain) → motor neuron → effector. (1 mark) When bright light falls on the eye: the light-sensitive receptors (photoreceptors) in the retina detect the stimulus → a sensory neuron carries the impulse to the brain, where a relay neuron in the mid-brain processes it (the pupillary reflex is a cranial reflex, so this relay is in the brain rather than the spinal cord) → the relay neuron passes the impulse to a motor neuron → the motor neuron carries the impulse to the effector, the circular muscles of the iris → these muscles contract and the pupil becomes smaller, reducing the light entering the eye. (2 marks) The whole response happens without conscious thought.

pyq.q: Explain the feedback mechanism that regulates the action of hormones, taking insulin as an example.
pyq.answer: The timing and amount of a hormone released are regulated by a feedback mechanism: the effect of the hormone itself controls how much more of it is secreted. (1 mark) Example: after a meal, the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood rises. This rise is detected by the cells of the pancreas, which respond by secreting more insulin. Insulin lowers the blood sugar. As the blood sugar level falls, the pancreas cells detect the fall and reduce the secretion of insulin. (2 marks) In this way blood sugar is kept within a narrow range. If insulin is not secreted in proper amounts, the sugar level rises and diabetes results.

pyq.q: Why is chemical communication considered better than electrical impulses as a means of communication between cells in a multicellular organism? Explain.
pyq.answer: Electrical impulses have two limitations. (i) They can reach only those cells that are directly connected by nervous tissue; cells not connected to a nerve cannot be reached. (ii) Once a neuron has fired an impulse, it takes some time to reset before it can generate the next one, so a cell cannot send impulses continuously. (2 marks) Chemical communication overcomes both. A hormone released into the blood reaches every cell of the body, and it can be secreted steadily for as long as needed; target cells that have the ability to detect the hormone respond to it. This makes chemical communication a better means for slow, widespread and continuous control such as growth and metabolism. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What are plant hormones? Name the plant hormones responsible for (i) growth of the stem, (ii) cell division, (iii) inhibition of growth, (iv) elongation of cells.
pyq.answer: Plant hormones (phytohormones) are chemical compounds synthesised in one part of a plant and diffused to another part, where they help to coordinate growth, development and responses to the environment. (1 mark) (i) Gibberellin (ii) Cytokinin (iii) Abscisic acid (iv) Auxin. (½ mark each)

pyq.q: A doctor advised a 60-year-old man to reduce sugar in his diet after a blood test showed a high level of glucose. (a) Name the disease, the hormone involved and the gland that secretes it. (b) Why are some patients of this disease given injections of the hormone? (c) Explain how the secretion of this hormone is regulated in a healthy person. (d) Name one other hormone secreted by an endocrine gland and state its function.
pyq.answer:
(a) The disease is diabetes. The hormone is insulin, secreted by the pancreas. (1½ marks)

(b) In diabetes the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, so blood sugar stays high and causes harmful effects. Injecting insulin supplies the missing hormone and brings blood sugar under control. It is injected rather than swallowed because insulin is a protein and would be digested. (1 mark)

(c) By a feedback mechanism. When blood sugar rises after a meal, the cells of the pancreas detect the rise and secrete more insulin, which lowers the sugar level. When the sugar level falls, the pancreas cells reduce insulin secretion. Thus the amount of insulin released is matched to the amount of sugar in the blood. (1½ marks)

(d) Any one: thyroxine from the thyroid gland regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; growth hormone from the pituitary regulates growth and development; adrenaline from the adrenal glands prepares the body for emergencies by raising heart rate and breathing rate. (1 mark)

pyq.q: (a) Define hydrotropism. Design an experiment to demonstrate this phenomenon. (b) Name three plant hormones and write one function of each.
pyq.answer:
(a) Hydrotropism is the directional growth movement of a plant part, usually the root, in response to water; roots grow towards water, showing positive hydrotropism. (1 mark)

Experiment: Take two trays (A and B) filled with moist soil and sow a few seedlings in each. In tray A, bury a porous clay pot filled with water near one edge. Tray B has no pot and serves as the control. Keep both under identical conditions for a few days. Observation: in tray A the roots are seen to bend and grow towards the porous pot; in tray B the roots grow straight downward. Conclusion: roots grow towards water, that is, they are positively hydrotropic. A labelled sketch of tray A with the pot and the bending roots earns the diagram credit. (2 marks)

(b) Auxin: promotes elongation of cells and is responsible for phototropism and coiling of tendrils. Gibberellin: helps in the growth of the stem. Cytokinin: promotes cell division, especially in fruits and seeds. (Abscisic acid, which inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves, may be given instead.) (2 marks)

pyq.q: (a) What is a reflex arc? Draw a labelled diagram of the reflex arc involved when a hand touches a hot object. (b) Show, as a flowchart, the sequence of events that occur when a person sneezes after dust enters the nose.
pyq.answer:
(a) A reflex arc is the path along which nerve impulses travel during a reflex action, from the receptor through the sensory neuron to the spinal cord, then through the motor neuron to the effector. (1 mark)

Diagram: draw the cross-section of the spinal cord; a hand near a flame; the heat receptor in the skin; the sensory neuron entering the spinal cord; the relay neuron inside; the motor neuron leaving to the arm muscle; arrows from receptor to effector and a branch marked to brain. Labels required: receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector (muscle). (2 marks)

(b) Dust enters the nose (stimulus) → receptors in the lining of the nose are stimulated → sensory neuron carries the impulse to the central nervous system (medulla/spinal cord) → relay neuron passes it to the motor neuron → motor neuron carries the impulse to the effectors (muscles of the diaphragm, chest and throat) → these muscles contract suddenly → air is expelled forcefully through the nose: the sneeze. (2 marks)

pyq.q: (a) Draw a neat labelled diagram of the human brain. (b) Write one function each of the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla. (c) How is the brain protected from injury and shock?
pyq.answer:
(a) Draw the side view of the brain with the cerebrum (large, wrinkled, front and top), the cerebellum (smaller, wrinkled, at the back below the cerebrum), the pons (in front of the cerebellum), the medulla (below the pons, continuing into the spinal cord) and the pituitary gland hanging below the fore-brain. Label cerebrum, cerebellum, pons, medulla, pituitary gland, spinal cord and mark fore-brain, mid-brain, hind-brain. (2 marks)

(b) Cerebrum: the thinking part of the brain; receives sensory information (hearing, sight, smell), stores memory and controls voluntary actions. Cerebellum: responsible for the precision of voluntary actions and for maintaining posture and balance of the body. Medulla: controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, heartbeat, salivation and vomiting. (2 marks)

(c) The brain is enclosed in a bony box, the skull (cranium). Inside the skull it is surrounded by cerebrospinal fluid, which acts as a shock absorber and protects the brain from jolts. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Meera's grandmother was found to have high blood sugar. The doctor explained that a hormone made by one of her organs was not being produced in sufficient quantity, and that in a healthy person the amount of this hormone released is adjusted according to the level of sugar in the blood. He prescribed daily injections of the hormone and advised her to reduce sugar in her diet.
(i) Name the hormone and the organ that secretes it.
(ii) Name the disease Meera's grandmother is suffering from.
(iii) Explain how the amount of this hormone released is adjusted in a healthy person.
(iv) Why is the hormone given as an injection and not as a tablet?
pyq.answer:
(i) The hormone is insulin; it is secreted by the pancreas. (1 mark)

(ii) Diabetes, caused by insufficient secretion of insulin, so that blood sugar rises. (1 mark)

(iii) By feedback control. When the blood sugar level rises, the cells of the pancreas detect it and secrete more insulin, which brings the level down. As the sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced. So the amount secreted is matched to the need. (1 mark)

(iv) Insulin is a protein. If taken by mouth it would be digested by the enzymes of the stomach and intestine and would not reach the blood, so it must be injected. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. Two students did an experiment. Student A kept a potted plant near a window so that light reached it from one side only; after a week the shoot had bent towards the window. Student B touched the leaves of a chhui-mui (Mimosa) plant and saw them fold within a few seconds. Both students said their plant had shown movement, but the teacher pointed out that the two movements are of different kinds.
(i) Name the type of movement shown by the plant of student A and the hormone responsible.
(ii) Explain how this hormone causes the shoot to bend.
(iii) How does the Mimosa leaf move, since a plant has no muscles?
(iv) State two differences between the two movements.
pyq.answer:
(i) Phototropism (positive phototropism of the shoot), a tropic or growth movement. The hormone is auxin. (1 mark)

(ii) Auxin is synthesised at the shoot tip. When light comes from one side, auxin diffuses to the shady side of the shoot. Auxin makes cells grow longer, so the cells on the shady side elongate more than those on the lit side, and the shoot bends towards the light. (1 mark)

(iii) The cells at the base of the Mimosa leaflets change the amount of water in them. When touched, these cells lose water, shrink and change shape, so the leaf folds. Information about the touch is passed from cell to cell by electrical-chemical means, without nerves. (1 mark)

(iv) The shoot movement is directional (towards light), slow and due to growth; the Mimosa movement is non-directional (does not depend on the direction of touch), rapid and independent of growth, being caused by change in water content of cells. (Any two, ½ mark each)

practice_mcq.q: Olfactory receptors are located in the:
practice_mcq.explanation: Olfactory receptors detect smell and are present in the nose; gustatory receptors on the tongue detect taste.

practice_mcq.q: The longest fibre on the cell body of a neuron is called the:
practice_mcq.explanation: The axon is the single long fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body; dendrites are short and branched.

practice_mcq.q: In a reflex arc, the neuron that carries the impulse from the spinal cord to the muscle is the:
practice_mcq.explanation: The motor (efferent) neuron carries the impulse from the spinal cord to the effector; the sensory neuron brings it in and the relay neuron connects the two.

practice_mcq.q: Reflex arcs are formed in the:
practice_mcq.explanation: Nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle in the spinal cord, where the sensory and motor neurons are connected through relay neurons to form reflex arcs.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the hind-brain?
practice_mcq.explanation: The cerebrum is the main part of the fore-brain. The hind-brain consists of the cerebellum, pons and medulla.

practice_mcq.q: The feeling of being full after a meal is due to a centre in the:
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states that the sensation of fullness comes from a centre associated with hunger, which is in a separate part of the fore-brain.

practice_mcq.q: The cerebrospinal fluid around the brain acts as a:
practice_mcq.explanation: The brain sits in a fluid-filled balloon inside the skull; the fluid absorbs shocks so that jolts are not transmitted to the brain.

practice_mcq.q: Muscle cells move when a nerve impulse arrives because:
options: Special proteins in them change shape and arrangement
practice_mcq.explanation: Special proteins in the muscle cell change their shape and arrangement in response to the electrical impulse, making the cell shorter.

practice_mcq.q: The folding of Mimosa leaves on touch occurs because the cells:
practice_mcq.explanation: The Mimosa response is independent of growth; cells at the base of the leaflets lose water, shrink and change shape.

practice_mcq.q: The growth of a pollen tube towards the ovule is an example of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Chemotropism is growth in response to a chemical stimulus; the pollen tube grows towards chemicals released by the ovule.

practice_mcq.q: A potted plant is laid on its side. After a few days the shoot bends upward. This shows that the shoot is:
practice_mcq.explanation: The shoot grows away from the pull of gravity, which is negative geotropism; the root would bend downward, showing positive geotropism.
NCERT states that auxin is synthesised at the shoot tip, from where it diffuses to the shady side of the shoot.

practice_mcq.q: Which plant hormone is present in higher concentration in fruits and seeds?
practice_mcq.explanation: Cytokinins promote cell division and are found where cells divide rapidly, such as in fruits and seeds.

practice_mcq.q: Wilting of leaves is an effect of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Abscisic acid is the growth-inhibiting plant hormone named in NCERT and its effects include wilting of leaves.

practice_mcq.q: When adrenaline is secreted, which of the following does NOT happen?
options: Blood flow to the digestive system increases
Blood is diverted to the skeletal muscles
practice_mcq.explanation: Adrenaline contracts the small arteries of the digestive system and skin, so blood flow to the gut decreases, not increases.

practice_mcq.q: Goitre is caused by deficiency of:
practice_mcq.explanation: Iodine is needed by the thyroid to make thyroxine; without it the gland swells, producing goitre.

practice_mcq.q: The hormone that brings about changes at puberty in females is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Oestrogen from the ovaries causes the changes of puberty in females; testosterone from the testes does so in males.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about nervous control is correct?
options: It is slower than hormonal control
Its effects last longer than those of hormones
It reaches only cells connected by nervous tissue
practice_mcq.explanation: Nerve impulses reach only cells connected to nervous tissue; nervous control is fast and short-lived, while hormones regulate growth and metabolism.

common_mistakes: Reversing the direction of the impulse in the neuron or synapse. The impulse always goes dendrite to cell body to axon end, and crosses the synapse from the axon end of one neuron to the dendrite of the next; the examiner checks the arrow.

Writing that the brain controls reflex actions. The reflex arc is formed in the spinal cord; the brain only receives the information afterwards. Say the brain is not involved in producing the reflex, but is informed of it.
Mixing up the cerebellum and the cerebrum. Cerebrum thinks; cerebellum balances. Riding a bicycle and walking in a straight line belong to the cerebellum, not the cerebrum.

Saying that the sensitive plant moves by growth or by hormones. Mimosa moves by change in the water content of its cells; it is the shoot bending towards light that is a growth movement caused by auxin.
Placing auxin on the lit side. Auxin diffuses to the shady side, the shady side grows longer, and that is why the shoot bends towards the light. Get the side wrong and the whole explanation fails.

Assigning the wrong function to a plant hormone: gibberellin for cell division or cytokinin for stem growth. Gibberellin is stem growth, cytokinin is cell division, abscisic acid is inhibition and wilting.
Giving only one change for adrenaline. The three-mark answer needs heart rate, diversion of blood from gut and skin to muscles, and breathing rate. One change earns one mark.
Forgetting the feedback direction in the insulin answer. Sugar rises, insulin rises, sugar falls, insulin falls. Write both halves of the loop.
Answering hormone questions without the gland. Every hormone answer should have gland, function and deficiency effect; a bare hormone name is rarely worth full marks.
strategy:
This is a chapter of names, sequences and three diagrams, and it rewards tidy memorisation over deep problem-solving. Spend the first hour on the nervous system: draw the neuron, the reflex arc and the brain from memory until every label is right, then write out the reflex arc sequence as a flowchart three times. These three drawings and the sequence cover most of the 3-mark and 5-mark questions asked in the last ten years.

Second, make a two-column table of brain parts against functions (cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla, pons, fore-brain hunger centre) and a three-column table of hormones against gland and deficiency effect (growth hormone, thyroxine, insulin, adrenaline, testosterone, oestrogen). Add a fourth table for the four plant hormones with their single job and the four tropisms with an example each. These tables are the raw material of every 1-mark and 2-mark question.

Third, learn the four standard comparisons in point form: reflex action versus walking, reflex versus involuntary action, Mimosa movement versus shoot bending, nervous versus hormonal control. Each has appeared as a 2- or 3-marker and will again.

In the exam, give this chapter about 15 minutes. For a 5-mark question, draw the diagram first (it is the easiest 2 marks), then write the explanation in numbered points. For 3-markers, three separate points, each a full sentence. Do not write essays; the marking scheme is a checklist.
